Logistics Nodes, filters and upgrades you place come out of storage, and whatever is missing is built as an ordinary SCC job, planned on your side and visible in the job list. This works anywhere, not only near your base: while you use the wrench, SCC keeps the controller's area loaded for half a minute.
scc.guide.integrations.ln4: The link asks the Security Terminal like every other access: take out, put in and order. With both AE2 and Refined Storage installed the wrench reads "AE2/SCC" - Logistics Networks only has those two names to give.
scc.guide.integrations.ln5: Moved or rebuilt the controller? The wrench still points at the old spot and finds nothing: no "+" for upgrades, no nodes from storage. Shift + right-click the new Calculator Controller - SCC removes the old link and the wrench links to the new one.
scc.guide.integrations.mek1: Mekanism's conversion recipes are read out of JEI: the network knows that a chemical comes from an item and counts the item as the ingredient. That is enough for ore processing chains where the gas only exists between two machines.
scc.guide.integrations.mek2: Chemicals can be made by an order: if the item for a chemical is not in storage (Flint for Oxygen, Salt for Hydrogen Chloride), the order makes the chemical first with an Electrolytic Separator or Chemical Infuser in the network - the byproduct (hydrogen) goes into storage. Moving gases outside of orders is still the job of the Transfer Calculator.
scc.guide.integrations.mek3: Chemicals - gases, slurries, infusions, pigments - count as a resource of the network:
scc.guide.integrations.mek4: A Storage Connector facing a machine with chemical tanks stores what is in them. Access direction and priority work exactly as they do for items.
scc.guide.integrations.mek5: The Transfer Calculator moves chemicals in and out. Put a filled chemical container - a Chemical Tank, a Gauge Dropper - into a filter field and right-click it until the green bubble shows: the field then means the chemical inside, not the container.
scc.guide.integrations.mek6: An empty import list takes every chemical the machine offers, the same rule as for items and fluids. The export list needs a field per chemical.
scc.guide.integrations.mek7: A Chemical Storage holds them without any machine in front of it. One tank per chemical, six tiers, and Mekanism's own pipes push into it and pull out of it directly.
scc.guide.integrations.mekkinds: The four kinds, in Mekanism's own words: gases (hydrogen, oxygen, chlorine, steam, ethene), slurries (the dirty and clean ore slurries of the 4x ore chain), infusion types (redstone, carbon, diamond, refined obsidian, bio, tin, fungi, gold), and pigments (one per dye colour, plus the ones from the Pigment Extractor). Since Mekanism 10.7 they are one registry, so anything another mod registers there works here too.
scc.guide.integrations.mekstore: Chemical Storage - the network's own tank for gases. Mekanism counts every chemical in the same registry, so one block takes all four kinds side by side.
scc.guide.integrations.none: And if none of them is installed?
scc.guide.integrations.none1: Then SCC runs exactly as it is: storage, terminals, autocrafting from vanilla recipes, wireless, breaking and transfer. Everything on this page is an addition, never a requirement.
scc.guide.integrations.powah1: The Energizing Socket is a compact base for Powah's Energizing Orb. Place the orb on top of it and put real Energizing Rods into its 8 slots (right-click with a rod, or open it and shift-click). Each rod gives the orb exactly what it gives in the usual setup - same rate per tier, read from Powah's config (by default 100 FE/t for Starter up to 200,000 FE/t for Nitro), with the same 1-second warm-up. Without rods it charges nothing.
scc.guide.integrations.powah2: Power comes from an SCC cable next to it (machines group of the network) or from any other mod's cable straight into the socket. Its buffer is as big as the rods' buffers together. A Processing Calculator facing the orb loads the ingredients and takes out the result as usual - the orb stays the machine.
scc.guide.integrations.powah3: The only gain is space: everything fits into two blocks. Real rods placed around the orb still charge it as usual. Only available with Powah installed.
scc.guide.integrations.qed1: The QED offers no inventory to the outside at all - for every pipe in the world it looks empty. SCC lays its own handler over the container the block does have, so a Processing Calculator in front of it can feed it like any other machine.
scc.guide.integrations.quests1: Item tasks are filled from the network. FTB Quests normally only ever looks at your inventory; SCC offers it what is in storage instead, so a quest that wants 512 iron does not mean carrying 512 iron around.
scc.guide.integrations.quests2: Tasks that must be crafted by hand, tasks with no maximum and quests that are not startable yet are left alone. What was skipped and why is written into the log after every pass.
scc.guide.integrations.raven1: Put a Processing Calculator in front of an Enchanting Table of the Raven: infusion recipes from JEI/EMI are planned like any other machine recipe. For each item SCC sets the table's Eterna, Quanta and Arcana to what the recipe needs, infuses it like the third option in the table's window, and sets your own values back right afterwards.
scc.guide.integrations.raven2: Nothing is free: every infusion takes 3 Lapis Lazuli and the experience for the table's level (liquid experience, 20 mB per point) from the network, as by hand. If something is missing, the order says what. A normal enchanting table works too: there the values of its bookshelves count, as by hand. If they do not fit the recipe, the order says what is missing (for example "Eterna 45 needed, table has 30").
scc.guide.integrations.rs1: A Storage Connector works on any block of a Refined Storage network - controller, cable, disk drive, storage block or interface. Everything the RS network stores shows up in the SCC terminal, and you can take out and put in from there.
scc.guide.integrations.rs2: Everything the RS network has a pattern for is listed as craftable and carries a small RS mark. Order it and SCC hands the job to RS instead of building it itself - RS takes the ingredients from its own storage, and the result lands in the RS storage the terminal already shows. "Max" in the order window asks RS how many it can build.
scc.guide.integrations.rs3: And the other way round: point an RS External Storage at a Network Antenna or a Calculator Controller, and RS sees the whole SCC network - read, insert, extract. Both directions between the same two networks are safe; nothing is counted twice.
scc.guide.integrations.rs4: Only items cross over, just like with AE2, and items a running SCC job has reserved stay where they are. If AE2 has a pattern for the same item too, the job goes to AE2.
scc.guide.integrations.souls1: Soul Storage, six tiers, crafted from Sculk around a Soul Pipe. Souls are a resource of the network like Source: the terminal shows them as their own line, a Storage Monitor shows them after a right-click with any Industrial Foregoing Souls block.
scc.guide.integrations.souls2: The SCC Interface connects Soul Pipes. Supply (the default) hands the network's souls to the pipes and tops up a Soul Pipe or Soul Surge right next to it. Accept takes souls from the pipes instead - for a Soul Laser Base at the far end. There is no "both": a pipe always pushes before it pulls, so the souls would just bounce back and forth.
scc.guide.integrations.souls3: Getting souls in: put a Storage Connector on top of a Soul Laser Base - its buffer counts as network storage - or a Transfer Calculator, which moves them into your Soul Storage. Any Industrial Foregoing Souls block in a Transfer Calculator filter stands for souls.
scc.guide.integrations.van1: Not every integration is another mod. Some vanilla blocks cannot simply be filled:
scc.guide.integrations.van2: Smithing table - has no inventory at all, it is a menu. The calculator brings its own.
scc.guide.integrations.van3: Stonecutter - the same, and it can make twenty things out of one stone; which one is decided by the job.
scc.guide.integrations.van4: Brewing stand - three bottles are one batch and the result comes in stages. The lock mode "empty" is meant for exactly that.
scc.guide.integrations.van5: Furnaces - fuel is handled separately from ingredients, and an upgrade slot is never mistaken for an output.
scc.guide.integrations.van6: Comparator - every own storage block answers a comparator with its exact fill level.
scc.guide.integrations.vanilla: Vanilla blocks that need special treatment
scc.guide.integrations.vill1: A trading block in front of a Processing Calculator turns a villager into a machine: the network puts in the payment and takes the result.
scc.guide.integrations.vill2: Offers are read directly from the villager, so mod-added trades work too.
scc.guide.integrations.vill3: A villager that has not traded yet can be re-rolled until the wanted offer appears - the same rule the mod's own button uses.
scc.guide.integrations.vill4: Enchanted books are listed from the tradeable tag instead of being rolled - otherwise only a handful of the forty enchantments would ever show up.
scc.guide.integrations.vill5: A trade can also be the preferred way for an item: pick "Villager trade" in the recipe choice of the crafting tree (or as a step of a Logic Calculator route) - then emeralds come from your sticks instead of unpacking emerald blocks.
scc.guide.integrations.what: What SCC knows about other mods
scc.guide.integrations.what1: SCC is built so that it works on its own and gets better when other mods are there. Every integration on this page is optional: if the mod is missing, nothing here runs, nothing is loaded, and nothing breaks. None of them is a hard dependency.
scc.guide.integrations.what2: Most of them go through reflection and are read out of the other mod at runtime - that way a mod update can at worst make one feature go quiet, never crash the game.
scc.guide.network.antenna: A full crafting terminal that nobody has to stand at - wireless terminals log in here. Range is 32 blocks, plus 32 for every Range Upgrade you put in, up to eight of them. With a Dimensional Upgrade neither distance nor dimension matters any more.
scc.guide.network.cable: Connects, and does nothing else. The cheapest block in the mod to place and the cheapest to run.
scc.guide.network.collector: Vacuums items lying on the ground into the network. Right-click it to set the range (1-8 blocks), how often it looks, and a filter for what it may pick up; the window can draw the area as a box in the world so you can see exactly what it covers. It leaves alone anything that is still too fresh to pick up.
scc.guide.network.controller: One per network, and there is no network without it. It lists every connected block grouped by type together with what each group draws, and it is the single point where FE goes in. A second controller in the same network (for example one joined through a Wireless Receiver) rests: only the first one pays for power, and the window of the resting one says which controller runs the network. If you would rather not have the requirement at all, turn it off with /scc requireController off.
scc.guide.network.how1: Every block of this mod is a network node. Two nodes belong to the same network if they touch, or if a chain of cable connects them. Cable is only there to cover distance - a terminal placed straight onto the controller works just as well.
scc.guide.network.how2: The network is walked fresh whenever something needs to know what is in it. That is why adding a block anywhere simply works: there is nothing to re-link and nothing to register.
scc.guide.network.rx: Continues the network wherever you put it down. Right-click a transmitter with it first, then place it - everything cabled to the receiver joins the transmitter's network. Both sides become one network: every terminal sees all storage on both sides, and one Calculator Controller is enough. To keep two networks apart and only move items, put a chest between them: a Transfer Calculator of one network fills it, a Storage Connector of the other reads it.
scc.guide.network.rxload: Both ends have to be loaded. The receiver never force-loads chunks, so a bridge into a base nobody is near is simply asleep until something loads it.
scc.guide.network.sky1: The whole network as a star map: every block is a star in the colour of its kind, the cables are the lines between them, and the glow shows the tier. Open it from the Map tab of the Calculator Controller, from the report of the Network Tool, or from the radial menu of the Wrench.
scc.guide.network.sky2: A sparkling star is working. A yellow ring means the storage is almost full, a blinking red ring means a problem - hover it for the reason. Grey stars without glow were switched off by load shedding, or the network is offline.
scc.guide.network.sky3: Hover a star for details. Click it to open its window if it is within reach; otherwise it is highlighted in the world, through walls. Shift-click always highlights.
scc.guide.network.sky4: Drag to move, mouse wheel to zoom, drag with the right mouse button to turn and tilt. Blocks behind a Wireless Receiver in another dimension appear as a separate group.
scc.guide.network.sky5: Very large networks are thinned out: straight cable runs become one line, and at most 2,000 stars are shown.
scc.guide.network.tx: Sits inside a network and broadcasts it. Takes Range Upgrades the same way the antenna does, and a Dimensional Upgrade to reach other worlds.
scc.guide.network.txwindow: Right-click a transmitter with an empty hand to open its window: range, whether it is your default transmitter, and every linked receiver with position, dimension, distance and state.
scc.guide.network.txwindow2: Moved your base? "Move all my receivers here" relinks every receiver you placed - in all dimensions, also in unloaded chunks - to this transmitter and makes it your default. It asks twice before it does anything.
scc.guide.network.txwindow3: Only your own receivers are moved. A receiver in an unloaded chunk switches over by itself the next time it loads; the window lists every receiver with what happened and why.
scc.guide.network.txwindow4: Receivers placed before 1.6 belong to the owner of the network they are linked to. If that cannot be found out, they are left alone - relink them once by hand.
scc.guide.observatory.analyzer: For a quick look at one block or the whole network the Network Tool and the network check in the terminal stay the fastest way - the observatory is for the long view.
scc.guide.observatory.block: Factory analysis for your network: where it jams, what would help and how it developed. Connect it with a cable, right-click to open.
scc.guide.observatory.estimate1: For every kind of order (Bronze, Steel ...) the network notes how long such orders stood at which machine type, and whether that work could have run in parallel (several runs left, or other orders waiting for the same machine). If orders spent 80 % of their time at one Alloy Smelter and all of it could be split, a second one halves that part: the orders finish about 40 % sooner.
scc.guide.observatory.estimate2: It is an estimate: it assumes the new machine is as fast as the old one and its ingredients arrive in time. If ingredients are short, the next bottleneck is the supply.
scc.guide.observatory.holo1: Above the block floats a hologram with the last hour: load, the busiest machine type, orders per hour, power balance and warnings. Cyan means all is well, yellow a bottleneck or warning, red that the network stands still.
scc.guide.observatory.record: You do not need the block for the recording: every network with a Calculator Controller records from the moment it is built - a few machines per second, so even huge networks do not lag. Kept are 12 x 5 minutes, 48 hours and 30 days; the data stays when the world is saved.
scc.guide.observatory.record2: Recorded are Processing Calculators with their machine, the Star Forge, Calculation Crafters and Transfer Calculators. Server owners can switch it off with /scc factoryLog off.
scc.guide.observatory.st.block: Blocked: machine full, output full, no power or no machine in front.
scc.guide.observatory.st.idle: Idle: free for the next order.
scc.guide.observatory.st.wait: Waiting: for ingredients, a redstone signal, a paused order or its turn.
scc.guide.observatory.st.work: Working: the machine runs for an order or by itself.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.bottlenecks: Bottlenecks: machine types by load, below the suggestions with estimated gain and the reasoning behind it.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.energy: Energy: generation, use, storage level, use per group and the machines that draw the most.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.history: History: load, orders, power, blocked share and lead time as curves - top right you choose 1 hour, 24 hours or 30 days.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.machines: Machines: a time bar per machine - green working, yellow waiting, red blocked, grey idle. Hover for the reasons, click to highlight it in the world.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.map: Map: the network from above or at an angle. Machines are colored by load, jams pulse red. Drag to move, scroll to zoom.
scc.guide.observatory.tab.overview: Overview: load, finished orders, lead time and power balance; the busiest machine types and the most important hints.
scc.guide.orderlists.blueprint: Blueprints: material list to order list
scc.guide.orderlists.blueprint1: Import Blueprint... (terminal menu, or below the lists) reads what a build needs: Litematica (.litematic), Create and structure block files (.nbt), WorldEdit (.schem), Litematica material lists (.txt/.csv), a list pasted from the clipboard, or the copy in a Building Gadgets 2 Copy-Paste Gadget, Template or Redprint.
scc.guide.orderlists.blueprint2: Files are found in scc_blueprints and schematics in the game folder, in config/litematica and among the structures of the world. Blocks become items: a double slab is two slabs, a door or bed one item; water, lava and air are skipped.
scc.guide.orderlists.blueprint3: The preview shows needed, in the network, missing and whether there is a recipe. Save as List makes a new top-up order list; Order Missing saves it and orders what is missing right away.
scc.guide.orderlists.blueprint4: Litematica is not needed to read .litematic files. For a build that is half done, export Litematica's material list (Write to file) - its Missing column counts only what is not placed yet.
scc.guide.orderlists.clipboard1: The Schematicannon prints what a schematic still needs as a Material Checklist - onto a Clipboard or into a book, whichever you put in its print slot. Keep the checklist in your hand, your inventory or the network's storage, open the order lists in a terminal and click From Clipboard: every line that is not ticked off becomes a line of a new list, named after the checklist.
scc.guide.orderlists.clipboard2: The new list tops up: what is already in storage or on its way is not crafted again. Order all crafts the rest with the machines of the network - the same plans as any other order.
scc.guide.orderlists.clipboard3: Lines without a recipe or with missing ingredients stay red. Hover the status to see what is missing; the summary at the bottom adds up what the whole list lacks.
scc.guide.orderlists.clipboard4: Long lists (up to 256 lines) are checked a few lines per tick, so the game keeps running. A terminal runs 12 jobs and queues 32 more; what does not fit follows in waves while the window stays open - or click Order all again later.
scc.guide.orderlists.clipboard5: Even simpler: put an Interface next to the Schematicannon. The cannon then builds straight from the whole network - no checklist needed.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists1: An order list is a named batch order: "Base kit: 64 torches, 16 chests, 8 furnaces". Open it from the terminal's menu (the three dots in the toolbar on the left) - or pin it to the bar. One click on Order all orders every line - each line becomes its own job.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists2: Top up to: only what is missing is ordered. 64 torches with 40 in stock orders 24; items already on their way from running jobs count as there.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists3: Order extra: every line is crafted in full, no matter what is in stock.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists4: Fill a list from the network (Add item), from your inventory (lay out a kit once, then save it) or from your JEI bookmarks. Type amounts, or turn the mouse wheel over them.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists5: The status column is a preview: In stock, Craft 24, Missing, No recipe. Hover it to see what exactly is missing; click an item name to open it in the normal order window with the recipe tree.
scc.guide.orderlists.lists6: Lists belong to the network and are stored in the Calculator Controller: every terminal and wireless terminal of the network shows the same lists, and a Settings Card copies them to another network.
scc.guide.orderlists.watch1: Watch up to 32 items per network (second tab of the order list window). The Calculator Controller looks at their stock every few seconds and keeps a history: one point per minute for the last hour, one per 15 minutes for the last day.
scc.guide.orderlists.watch2: Hovering a watched item in the terminal shows its inflow per hour and a small chart.
scc.guide.orderlists.watch3: When nothing new arrives for 10 minutes (5 to 60, adjustable), the player who watches the item gets a message: "Iron Ingot farm stopped". Another message follows when it runs again.
scc.guide.orderlists.watch4: Set a minimum to get a warning when the stock falls below it. The bell button turns the messages off - the history keeps running.
scc.guide.orderlists.watch5: Only increases count as inflow. If the network uses up everything a farm delivers within a few seconds, the farm looks stopped. Items that never had any inflow are not reported.
scc.guide.overview.calc1: Every recipe your pack has is scanned into one catalogue - workbench recipes, furnace recipes, and the recipes of every machine JEI knows about. From that catalogue the mod can answer a single question all the way down: what does it actually take to make this?
scc.guide.overview.calc2: Ask for one netherite pickaxe and it knows about the diamonds, the sticks, the scrap and the gold - and if you let it, it will go and make all of them.
scc.guide.overview.can: What you can do with it
scc.guide.overview.can1: See every item in every attached container in one searchable list.
scc.guide.overview.can2: Order anything and let the network craft it - workbench recipes and machine recipes alike.
scc.guide.overview.can3: Attach almost any modded machine. The calculator works out what it is and feeds it.
scc.guide.overview.can4: Keep stock levels topped up on their own, turn stock counts into redstone, and watch every machine's load on one panel.
scc.guide.overview.can5: Reach the whole network wirelessly, and across dimensions if you pay for it.
scc.guide.overview.clicks: Click a picture in this manual to see its recipe in JEI or EMI - right-click shows what it is used for. Lines starting with » jump to another chapter.
scc.guide.overview.net: None of this works on its own. A network is a Calculator Controller plus everything connected back to it - that is the next chapter.
scc.guide.overview.what1: Super Cool Calculator turns the chests you already have into one storage network, and then takes over the tedious half of building things: it works out the complete recipe tree for whatever you ask for, pulls the ingredients out of storage, and drives the machines that make it.
scc.guide.overview.what2: There are no storage cells and no drives to build first. You put a Storage Connector on a chest, a barrel, a drawer or a tank, and its contents belong to the network from that moment on.
scc.guide.power.cmd1: All of it can be changed while the game runs, with /scc. Operator only - whether the network needs power is a rule of the world, not a personal setting.
scc.guide.power.cmd2: /scc list - every setting with its value
scc.guide.power.cmd4: /scc requireController on|off - whether a network needs a controller at all
scc.guide.power.cmd5: /scc powerFactor 0-10000 - all costs in percent. 100 is normal, 50 is half, 0 is free.
scc.guide.power.cmd6: /scc controllerCapacity and /scc controllerTransfer - buffer size and input rate
scc.guide.power.cmd7: /scc doctor - opens the network report: what is attached, and which recipe kinds this network cannot run, each with the blocks that would fix it. The same report sits behind the button in the Calculator Monitor, so you do not need the command to find it. For tracking problems down there is the Network Check (terminal menu or Network Tool window): every problem with its location, and a Mark button that highlights it in the world.
scc.guide.power.cmd8: /scc unstick - releases every step filter in the network around you. Use it when machines sit there full and every order says "no matching machine in the network": whatever is left inside goes back to storage and the machines are free again.
scc.guide.power.cmd9: /scc selftest - the mod checks itself. It looks for a free cube of air above you, places every block of the mod once, builds a small network, stores an item and takes it back out, paints a cable to prove that a colour splits a network - and clears everything away again. Failures show up in the chat, the full run in scc.log. Nothing outside that cube is touched.
scc.guide.power.costs1b: Multiplied by the tier: Basic 1x, Red Dwarf 1.5x, Yellow Star 2x, Blue Giant 3x, Neutron Star 4x, Singularity 6x. A grown base lands somewhere around 50 to 100 FE per tick - one photon harvester with a good lens, or one simple generator from another mod. The Stellar Distributor adds 0.1 FE/t for every block it supplies.
scc.guide.power.costs2: Reach costs extra on an antenna or a wireless transmitter: +4 FE/t per Range Upgrade, or 40 FE/t with Infinite Range, or 96 FE/t with a Dimensional Upgrade - only the farthest-reaching upgrade counts. The receiver pays nothing extra. The antenna's window and Jade show what it draws right now.
scc.guide.power.designs1: The whole mod comes in 27 designs - dark steel and gold by default, light, and colour worlds from Porcelain to Burgundy & Gold. Blocks, panels, cables and items all take on the design you pick, and the windows turn light or dark to match. Classic brings back the colours of the first versions: dark slate plates, black trims and grey symbols instead of gold.
scc.guide.power.designs2: Press F7 and open the Design list. The preview next to it shows a machine, a storage block and a cable in the design under your mouse; nothing changes until you press Apply, double-click or hit Enter. Then everything switches at once - no loading screen.
scc.guide.power.designs3: The Star Forge and the Sky Harvester take on the design too. The designs are recoloured while the game loads, so they cost no extra download.
scc.guide.power.designs4: The design belongs to your game, not to a world or a server, so it follows you everywhere. Other players on the same server see whichever design they picked.
scc.guide.power.designs5: Want a few blocks in a different design? The Design Brush paints single blocks - those look the same for everyone.
scc.guide.power.mode1: On by default: every block on the network costs FE per tick. The controller pays from its own buffer first, then from the network's Energy Storages. So you can feed it by cable into the controller, or put a Transfer Calculator in energy mode on a generator - that charges the Energy Storages (or the controller, if there are none), and the network runs on it. The controller never gives energy back, so no machine can drain it. Switch it off with /scc power off.
scc.guide.power.mode2: The network is billed once a second rather than every tick - walking the whole network twenty times a second would be the most expensive thing in the mod, and for a number that only changes when you build something. It also gets three failed payments of grace before it stops, so a short brownout does not cancel your orders.
scc.guide.power.settings1: Press F7 in game (or Mods > SCC > Config) for the switches you actually reach for: Star Forge and Sky Harvester animations, the sky objects, the window fade-in - and every SCC sound on its own, grouped, with a play button to hear it. Everything saves at once and works without a restart.
scc.guide.power.settings2: Two more keys under Controls > SCC, unbound by default, toggle the star animations and sounds directly and say On or Off above the hotbar.
scc.guide.power.upgradeall: The controller can also raise the whole network at once. Pick a tier at the bottom of its window: a confirmation shows which upgrade stones it needs, how many are in storage and how many the network can craft - and from that, how many blocks can be upgraded completely. Start upgrades exactly those, one block per second, with settings, facing and facade carried over, exactly as a stone in your hand would. It counts in single steps (Basic to Red Dwarf to Yellow Star and so on), because the shortcut stones all lead away from basic: in a network with mixed tiers they would never arrive.
scc.guide.power.upgradeall2: If the stones don't cover every block, a second window lets you choose who gets them first: put the groups in order - Processing Calculators before Storages, say - or untick a group to leave it for later. The controller remembers that order. It orders stones only for the chosen blocks and stops when they are done; if a stone can't be crafted after all, it stops right there and tells you what was missing instead of waiting forever.
scc.guide.processing.aa_reconstructor: Runs the Atomic Reconstructor from Actually Additions - a Processing Calculator no longer does that. Face it at the reconstructor from any side except the one its beam comes out of, or into the beam itself: an air block up to 10 blocks in front of the reconstructor, nothing solid in between. It lays the ingredients into the beam as floating items, nobody else can pick them up, and collects what the reconstructor turns them into. The reconstructor does the work as usual: it needs its CF, fires every 5 seconds and must not get a redstone signal (in pulse mode the calculator fires it itself, only while an item is in the beam - no clock needed). The lens decides the recipes: no lens or the plain Lens runs the reconstructor recipes from JEI (Iron Ingot to Enori Crystal, for example), the Lens of Color runs the color changes; with any other lens it runs nothing. Its window shows the lens, the beam, the power and what is in the beam right now; if a recipe needs a different lens, the order planner says so. One tier only: the reconstructor sets the pace.
scc.guide.processing.advanced_res: If the machine has a tank (or Mekanism is installed), the Routing tab shows switches for items, fluids and chemicals, each with its own sides - like the side configuration of Mekanism. Fluids and chemicals start on Automatic (SCC finds the side itself; on Mekanism machines it looks at every side). Set one side by hand and that kind only uses the sides you set: water in on the left, hydrogen out on top, oxygen out at the bottom. Auto puts a kind back to Automatic.
scc.guide.processing.altars1: Most altars and multiblock machines need nothing special: put a Processing Calculator against the block that does the crafting - the core, the altar or the controller - and connect it to the network. The recipes JEI/EMI shows for that block are then planned like any other machine recipe.
scc.guide.processing.altars2: Ingredients that belong on other blocks (pedestals, hatches): add a Routing Module and link those blocks as ports - shift-right-click the calculator with the Network Tool, then each block (up to 16). They are filled in the order you link them, right after the machine itself - for a fixed item on a fixed block, give each ingredient its own target port in the Custom Pattern Module.
scc.guide.processing.altars3: A recipe JEI does not show, or one with more than 9 ingredients: write it yourself with the Custom Pattern Module (up to 18 ingredients).
scc.guide.processing.altars4: The center item has to go in last: switch on Reverse insertion order - on the Routing tab for the whole calculator, or in a pattern for one recipe.
scc.guide.processing.altars5: Draconic Evolution Fusion Crafting: the calculator against the Fusion Crafting Core fills the core and every injector by itself and starts the fusion - no module, no ports (see Integrations).
scc.guide.processing.altars6: Blood Altar (Neo Vitae: Ara Vitae): the calculator against the altar puts in one item at a time and takes the result out as soon as it is done.
scc.guide.processing.altars7: SCC only carries the items. What the altar itself needs - power for the injectors, the Life Essence (LP) and tier of a Blood Altar, the right structure - you still provide yourself, just like crafting by hand.
scc.guide.processing.anvil1: Facing an Anvil, the calculator uses it with the vanilla rules - prior work penalty, Too Expensive! at 40 levels and wear on the anvil included. Set the left item and the right one; the right one decides what happens:
scc.guide.processing.anvil2: A repair material (Diamond for diamond gear) repairs the most damaged piece, but only once a quarter of its durability is gone, and uses just as much material as it needs.
scc.guide.processing.anvil3: The same item on the right: the two most damaged pieces are combined into one.
scc.guide.processing.anvil4: An enchanted book (or any other item) goes on the first piece in storage it actually improves.
scc.guide.processing.anvil5: The number is the level limit per use. Experience comes from the network (a 5-level repair costs 55 XP). When the anvil breaks, the station puts a new one from storage in its place, or orders one. It does not work out the cheapest order for combining many books - that stays a job for your own head.
scc.guide.processing.basic: Place it against a machine and it works out for itself which machine that is, from the block's own id - always, with or without modules. From then on the network sends that machine every recipe it can do, puts the ingredients in (fluids and chemicals a recipe needs included) and pulls the finished results back out. In the normal case there is nothing to set up. Against an Easy Villagers block it does the trading instead - see below.
scc.guide.processing.batch: Batch on the Machine tab says how many runs go in at once - any number from 1 to 4096. Click it to type a number, Shift-click doubles, right-click halves, and the mouse wheel over the button steps by one (Shift: eight, Ctrl: 64). Every ingredient is multiplied with it, and the lock only engages after the last run of the set. A big batch pays off at machines that hold more than a stack: factories with many slots or machines with large slots. Each slot only gets what the machine accepts - once it is full, the set ends there and nothing is lost.
scc.guide.processing.casting: Hephaestus casting: against a Casting Table the Processing Calculator lays the cast (ingot, nugget, gem ...) on the table itself - it stays there for the next pour - and fills the molten metal from the network's Fluid Storage; against a Casting Basin it pours and takes the block out. Molten metal is ordered from the network like any other fluid.
scc.guide.processing.composter: Composter: place a Processing Calculator against a Composter - any side works - and the network can make Bone Meal from anything compostable: seeds, saplings, leaves, crops. The calculator drops one item at a time into the Composter and takes the Bone Meal out as soon as it is ready. Each item only fills the Composter by chance, so the plan counts with the average (about 21 seeds or 7 cakes per Bone Meal) and adds more items if luck runs short. In the recipe choice for Bone Meal this shows up as Composting, one entry per chance, and the network uses whatever compostable item it has in storage.
scc.guide.processing.create: Create machines work on the block below them. Face the Processing Calculator at the Basin or the Depot, not at the machine: a Mechanical Mixer above the Basin mixes (Brass Ingot, Andesite Alloy), a Mechanical Press above the Basin compacts, and a Press above a Depot presses sheets. Ingredients go into the Basin and the results come back out of it; a Basin with nothing above still counts as a Basin. For heated recipes put a Blaze Burner under the Basin - the calculator feeds it from the network while such a recipe runs: coal, charcoal or wood (tag scc:blaze_burner_fuel), and Blaze Cake for superheated recipes, but only if the network has some. A fuel set in its window keeps the burner lit all the time. The Transfer Calculator can feed a Blaze Burner too: put the fuel in its export list.
scc.guide.processing.create_assembly: Sequenced Assembly (Precision Mechanism): put a Deployer two blocks above a Depot, pointing down, and face the Processing Calculator at the Depot. The calculator places the starting item (the Golden Sheet) on the Depot, keeps the parts in its own small store and hands the Deployer exactly the one part the next step needs, loop after loop. Only recipes made purely of deploying steps can run this way - ones with pressing, cutting or filling steps would need several machines and are not planned. Failed assemblies go to storage as scrap, and SCC runs extra attempts until the order is complete. Simple deploying recipes (a Shaft and planks into a Cogwheel) work at the same station.
scc.guide.processing.create_crafter: Mechanical Crafters and Crushing Wheels: face the Processing Calculator at any crafter of a grid (arrows as usual - the last crafter gives out the result). The calculator collects one full set, puts every item into exactly the crafter the recipe shape asks for and starts the grid like a redstone signal, so the grid may be bigger than the recipe - leftover crafters stay empty. One set at a time. It takes the result from the block the last crafter points into, or picks it up where the crafter threw it out; on a belt it is gone. Crushing Wheels: face the calculator at the gap between the two wheels (from above) or at one of the wheels. The ingredients go into the gap, and the calculator collects what falls out below, by-products included.
scc.guide.processing.create_fan: Encased Fan (bulk processing): face the Processing Calculator into the air stream of an Encased Fan, anywhere behind the block the fan blows through. Water washes, Lava or Fire blasts (smelts), a Campfire smokes, Soul Fire or a Soul Campfire haunts. The block in front of the calculator must be air or a Depot. In the air, the calculator keeps the ingredients floating in the stream in stacks of 16 until Create has processed them, then collects the results, side products included - nobody else can pick them up. With a Depot, the ingredients go onto the Depot and the results are taken from it. Each calculator only runs the recipes of its catalyst and shows up as Fan (Washing) and so on. The fan has to turn, and its stream only reaches as far as its speed allows: 4 blocks at 16 RPM, 20 blocks at 256 RPM. Fan types from add-ons work the same way - Freezing, Ending and Coloring from Create: Dragons Plus, for example; the calculator then shows the add-on's own name for them.
scc.guide.processing.create_more: More Create machines: a Spout two blocks above a Depot fills items - face the Processing Calculator at the Depot; the items go onto the Depot, and the fluid comes from the network's Fluid Storage into the Spout. A Mechanical Saw only cuts items when it faces up; the calculator may sit on any side of it, above or below as well, and takes the cut pieces itself - even the ones the saw has already thrown out next to it. An Item Drain empties buckets and bottles, with the calculator at any side of it or on top: the empty containers come back into storage, and the fluid goes into the network's Fluid Storage, so the drain never fills up.
scc.guide.processing.custom: Custom Pattern Module: recipes you write yourself, for machines JEI does not know. The Own recipes tab lists them - ingredients, arrow, result - with a pencil to edit and a bin to delete (Shift+click). New recipe opens the editor on the first free slot: click with the item, drag it from JEI, or take a whole JEI recipe with its + button. Scroll over a field to change its amount, or middle-click it and type the amount. Shift + middle-click an ingredient to mark it as staying in the machine - a press, a mold: it goes in once and is never used up. Results can be fluids, too. The network prefers these recipes over the ones from JEI.
scc.guide.processing.custom_book: Calculators with the Custom Pattern Module in front of the same kind of machine share one recipe book: save a recipe on one and they all have it, and an order may use any of them. Machines that need a template inside - an Inscriber with its press, a packer with its mold - each need different recipes: switch the chain button in the recipe window to Own, and that calculator keeps its own list that only it runs.
scc.guide.processing.custom_flow: Flow & targets (the beam button in the recipe editor): where each ingredient goes and when. Link the blocks around the machine on the map - or Shift + right-click them with the Network Tool - and each gets a number and a color. Click an ingredient, then a block: it goes there instead of into the machine. "One each" puts one item into every empty linked block (injectors, pedestals) - the same item may sit in several places. Drag ingredients into later waves; they follow after the wave delay, optionally only once the previous wave is processed. For the whole recipe: a redstone pulse or a signal until the result (to start altars), wait for a redstone signal or for energy, collect the result from a linked block, runs per set, cycle time, timeout, priority for the planner, and an own name and icon.
scc.guide.processing.custom_flow2: Templates set it up in one click. Fusion Crafting (Draconic Evolution): catalyst as the first ingredient, then the injector items (the + of a JEI recipe does that), choose "Fusion Crafting: core + injectors" - the calculator in front of the core, the injectors linked. A linked core works too: set it as the target of the catalyst and as "Result from", and put the calculator next to it so the redstone pulse reaches it.
scc.guide.processing.custom_machinery: Custom Machinery: face a Processing Calculator at a machine from Custom Machinery (made by a modpack's datapack or KubeJS script). All of these machines are the same block, so the calculator reads which machine it is and runs exactly that machine's recipes from JEI - items in, fluids from your tanks, results out. Power comes from your own cables, as with any other machine. Machines that use the crafting processor (you take the result out by hand) are not run.
scc.guide.processing.custom_more: A recipe can have up to 18 ingredients - the arrow button above the grid shows the second page (a + on it means there is something on the other page). A calculator can have up to 16 ports, enough for altars with one pedestal per ingredient.
scc.guide.processing.enchant1: A Processing Calculator facing an Enchanting Table works it like a player: set the item to enchant and how many enchanted ones to keep in storage. Below that number it takes a plain one from storage, adds Lapis Lazuli, pays with liquid experience from the network and puts the result back. Bookshelves around the table count exactly as they do for a player.
scc.guide.processing.enchant2: Costs follow the table: the network counts as a player standing exactly on the level the option asks for. The third option at 15 bookshelves needs 30 levels on hand (1395 XP, about 28 buckets of liquid experience) and uses up 3 of them (306 XP). "Best" takes the strongest option the network can afford, 1 to 3 fix the choice.
scc.guide.processing.enchant3: The results are random, just like at the table. There is no re-rolling and no target enchantment - sort the books with filters afterwards, or put them on gear with the anvil station. Books are ordered on their own when they run out; other items are not, so no diamond armor gets crafted behind your back.
scc.guide.processing.farmersdelight: Farmer's Delight: a Processing Calculator against a Cutting Board cuts with the tool the recipe asks for (knife, axe, shears ...). The tool comes from storage once and stays in the calculator until it breaks; by-products such as Tree Bark go into storage as well. The Cooking Pot works from any side: ingredients, bowls and the finished meal all go through the calculator - the pot only needs heat below it.
scc.guide.processing.furnace_xp: Furnaces, Smokers and Blast Furnaces only hand out their experience when a player empties the result slot - and with a calculator collecting the results, nobody ever does. So after collecting, the calculator puts that experience into the network as liquid experience, 20 mB per point: into a tank that already holds some, otherwise into any Fluid Storage with room. This needs a mod with liquid experience (Ender IO, Mob Grinding Utils, Just Dire Things and others). Whatever does not fit stays in the furnace, nothing is lost. The server setting furnaceXp turns this off.
scc.guide.processing.grill: Campfire, Soul Campfire and Farmer's Delight's Stove and Skillet have no inventory - a Processing Calculator placed against one brings its own. It lays the food on like a player would, waits for the cooking time and picks the result up again (only what it put on itself, nothing a player dropped). A campfire or stove must be lit, a skillet needs heat below it. Note: campfire recipes are blocked by default in the client config (blockedRecipeTypes), because nearly all of them copy furnace recipes - remove minecraft:campfire_cooking from that list to cook on campfires.
scc.guide.processing.intro: One block - the Processing Calculator - gets any machine working for the network. On its own it already does most of the work; three modules add what fussy machines, fuel and your own recipes need.
scc.guide.processing.legacy: Until 1.3 there were three blocks: the Processing, the Advanced and the Custom Processing Calculator. Old worlds convert on their own: every placed Advanced becomes a Processing Calculator of the same tier with the Routing and Supply Modules, every Custom one with all three - sides, ports, fuel, recipes and running orders stay. Old ones in SCC storage turn into a Processing Calculator plus its modules within a few seconds. Old ones in chests turn into the new block when placed, or craft one on its own (a Crafter works too) to get a Processing Calculator plus its modules. A Requester, order list or restock setting that asked for an old one now asks for the Processing Calculator of the same tier.
scc.guide.processing.modules1: The window opens on the Machine tab: the machine with its status, the switches for auto-pull, auto-drain and lock, batch, priority and the three module slots. An empty slot shows the module's shape faded. Click it: if the module is in storage (or in your inventory), it goes in at once. If not, the order window opens for it - Ctrl+click orders it right away without the window - and as soon as the order is done, the module goes in by itself. Shift+click takes a module out again, back into storage. Shift-clicking a module in your inventory puts it straight into its slot.
scc.guide.processing.modules2: Every module you put in gets its own tab at the top of the window, with the module as its icon - Routing, Supply, Own recipes. Without the module there is no tab and no greyed-out button. Taking a module out keeps its settings in the calculator: put it back in and everything is as before. A Settings Card copies the modules too - missing ones are taken from storage or ordered.
scc.guide.processing.modules3: The modules are cheap: iron, redstone or gold and one part that fits - a Hopper for Routing, a Furnace and a Bucket for Supply, a Book and Quill for Custom Pattern. With any module the calculator draws 1.5 FE/t instead of 1.0.
scc.guide.processing.pick1: Machine has an inventory and one face is enough - no module needed.
scc.guide.processing.pick2: Machine is fussy about sides, or is a multiblock with several hatches - Routing Module.
scc.guide.processing.pick3: Machine needs fuel or power kept topped up - Supply Module.
scc.guide.processing.pick4: Machine JEI does not know, or a recipe you want to write yourself - Custom Pattern Module.
scc.guide.processing.ports: Machines built from several blocks - a Modern Industrialization multiblock with separate hatches, a refinery that takes its fluid on another block - get ports (Routing Module). A port is a face of another block nearby that the calculator also uses: ingredients and fluids go in there too, results come out there too. Shift-right-click the calculator with the Network Tool, then shift-right-click each face you want: the first click makes it input + output, the next input only, then output only, then it is gone again. Beams show the ports while the tool is bound or the window is open. Clicking a port again with the Network Tool goes input, output, fuel only, removed - fuel only is where the Supply Module puts its fuel, for example the fuel hatch of a multiblock.
scc.guide.processing.ports2: The calculator still faces the block that decides the recipes - usually the controller. Items go into its own input sides first, then into the ports; fluids fill whichever input takes them. Results are collected as items only, so a fluid product needs another way to storage, such as a Transfer Calculator. Up to 8 ports within 16 blocks, and a Settings Card copies them to an identical build next to it.
scc.guide.processing.rechiseled: Chisels decorative blocks of the chisel mods - Rechiseled, Chisel and Chipped - for the network with no machine in front: it does the chisel's work itself. Order a variant (also blocks from addon groups such as Rechiseled: Chipped) in the terminal and the planner takes a base block of its group from storage - vanilla stone, planks, bricks and anything with a vanilla recipe - and puts the variant back; one block gives one variant, with Rechiseled one block gives two slabs. Blocks you have already chiseled are never used up as ingredients. Chipped's groups need no workbench next to it - in Chipped itself every table converts every group, too. Middle-click such a block in the world with a linked Wireless Terminal: if storage has it, it lands in your hand, if not, the order window opens for it. It costs 1.5 FE/t and chisels 16 pieces per second, faster with Job Accelerators. Recipe: Processing Calculator, a chisel (from Rechiseled, Chisel or Chipped), stone bricks and iron - only with one of these mods installed.
scc.guide.processing.routing: Routing Module: you decide which side of the machine the calculator may use. The Routing tab shows the machine as an unfolded cube with its real textures; the border and mark of each face say its mode - input, output, both, fuel only or off. Click a face for the next mode, right-click for the previous one. You need it whenever a machine only takes ingredients on top and only gives out at the bottom, or wants two different inputs. Press Auto and it asks the machine itself which face does what - on a furnace that gives input on top, output below and fuel on all four sides. Shift+click on Auto switches every side off, Ctrl+click turns every side one step further.
scc.guide.processing.smithing: The smithing table has no inventory of its own - it is a menu, not a machine. A Processing Calculator placed against one brings its own: template, base and addition go in, the network smiths with the real recipe, and the result comes back out. Netherite tools and armor trims are ordered like anything else.
scc.guide.processing.speed1: The Processing Calculator follows the normal tier ladder, with or without modules. The tier decides how fast it hands work over and how many jobs it holds at once - it does not make the machine behind it any faster.
scc.guide.processing.supply: Supply Module: keeps the machine supplied, whatever recipe runs. Set a fuel item on the Supply tab and the calculator keeps that many in the machine, ordering more when storage runs out; drag a fluid from JEI onto the field (or pick a bucket at a machine with a tank) for liquid fuel; the FE switch pushes power from the network into the machine, as fast as the tier allows - the bar next to it shows how full the machine is. A fuel set at a Basin keeps its Blaze Burner lit all the time - without the module the burner is only fed while a heated recipe runs.
scc.guide.processing.trading: Easy Villagers put a real villager in a block. Place a Processing Calculator against one and the network can trade: what the villager offers shows up in the terminal like anything else, and ordering it pays out of storage. Where a villager turns several things into emeralds - paper, wheat, carrots - the calculator's window lets you pin the one trade the network may use, so it sells what you actually farm instead of whatever came first in the list.
scc.guide.processing.wall: The Processing Calculator exists a second time as a small panel that lives inside the cable instead of taking a block of its own - with the same module slots - and so does the Transfer Calculator. Right-click the side of a cable with one and it moves in, keeping every connection the cable had; the panel goes against the machine, so a run of cable can pass straight through a wall of furnaces or chests. Twelve pixels across, so a facade over that cable leaves a rim around it. A shapeless recipe turns each one into its full block version and back, at every tier. A panel that moved into a cable keeps that cable inside it: break the panel and the cable drops with it, and the wrench leaves it lying instead. A panel placed straight onto a machine never had one, so it gives none back.
scc.guide.quarry.area1: Six numbers set the area relative to the core: Width and Length, Depth, and where it starts - Ahead (behind the core), Sideways and the Height of the top layer. Each tier has a maximum size. Height reaches up to the build limit - enough to take down a whole mountain next to your base. From 97 blocks on the quarry works chunk by chunk, each one all the way down.
scc.guide.quarry.area2: Click ±1, Shift ±16, Ctrl ±64, Ctrl+Shift ±256, or turn the mouse wheel over a row. Click a number to type it in; Enter or Tab confirms.
scc.guide.quarry.area3: While the window is open the whole box is drawn in the world with lasers; otherwise only its top frame.
scc.guide.quarry.area4: Before you start, the window counts the ores in the area (Estimate). While mining it shows what was found.
scc.guide.quarry.area5: Gravel and sand that slide into the pit are picked up at the end: the quarry only says Done when the area is really empty (apart from protected blocks).
scc.guide.quarry.cards1: Up to six card slots: Basic has one, every tier one more, the Singularity six. Locked slots show which tier opens them; cards in a slot the tier no longer has drop out onto the core. Each card adds a skill and costs extra FE per block.
scc.guide.quarry.comparator: A comparator at the core reads the progress: 0 before the first block, 1 to 14 while it mines, 15 when the area is done. Orbital Mining never ends and gives 0.
scc.guide.quarry.fill: Fill Holes - every mined spot is filled with cobblestone, cobbled deepslate, dirt or netherrack from storage. Together with Ores Only the landscape stays as it was.
scc.guide.quarry.fluids: Fluids - source blocks are pumped into the network if it has room, otherwise removed; flowing fluid goes too. Water or lava running in from outside the area is sealed off with cobblestone from storage. Without this card fluids are simply skipped.
scc.guide.quarry.fortune: Fortune - level I on Basic up to V on Singularity (+100% FE). With Silk Touch in too, Silk Touch wins.
scc.guide.quarry.marker: Quarry Marker - stakes out the area like BuildCraft landmarks: one in a corner, one each along X and Z at the same height. Right-click a marker to see the lines. Use markers in the window takes the area (one marker within 3 blocks of the core).
scc.guide.quarry.notice: When a pit is done, the player who placed the quarry gets a short notice with its position - if they are online.
scc.guide.quarry.orbital: Orbital Mining (endgame) - no hole at all: the quarry pulls the ores of its own dimension from orbit. More under Orbital Mining below.
scc.guide.quarry.orbital1: With the Orbital Mining card the quarry digs no hole. It reads the world generation of its own dimension and pulls the ores found there - mod ores included, for example Allthemodium in the Overworld, Vibranium in the Nether and Unobtainium in the End. Each ore comes about as often as the world generates it, so rare ores stay rare; higher tiers pull them a little more often.
scc.guide.quarry.orbital2: Items per haul follow the tier's loot table (data/scc/loot_table/quarry/orbital), so the power per item stays the same. A dimension without ore veins (vanilla End) uses that loot table directly. Below Blue Giant only ores the tier's pickaxe can harvest.
scc.guide.quarry.orbital3: Pack makers: data/scc/scc_balance/orbital/ores.json sets speed, FE per haul, weights and extra ores; the block tag scc:orbital_blacklist removes ores.
scc.guide.quarry.ores: Ores Only - mines blocks in the tag c:ores and leaves the rest standing (+10% FE).
scc.guide.quarry.output1: Connected to an SCC network by cable, everything goes straight into storage and the power comes from the network. Without a network the drops go into a chest next to the core, then into its own 9-slot buffer; feed it FE with any cable.
scc.guide.quarry.output2: Nothing is ever lost: when nothing fits any more, the quarry waits.
scc.guide.quarry.power1: Each block costs FE: 800 on Basic up to 2,500 on Singularity - the fast tiers pay more per block, so a Singularity quarry draws about 15,000 FE/t, a Basic one about 80 FE/t. Hard blocks cost more (obsidian about six times as much), plus the cards.
scc.guide.quarry.power2: With a network it fills its own buffer from storage in small portions - it shows up as Machines in the power overview.
scc.guide.quarry.power3: Air and filtered blocks cost nothing; up to 512 spots are checked per step.
scc.guide.quarry.power4: If the network delivers less, the quarry mines as fast as the power allows and says Not enough power - in its window and in Jade.
scc.guide.quarry.refill1: Refill pit (button on the side of the window): when the area is mined, the quarry fills it again from the bottom up with the fill block you chose (field left of your inventory, cobblestone by default). Only spots it dug out itself and caves below them are filled - the air above the old ground stays free.
scc.guide.quarry.refill2: Replace fluids: water and lava sources in the area become the fill block while mining - no lava lakes, no floods.
scc.guide.quarry.refill3: Each placed block costs a quarter of the mining price. Without fill blocks in the network it waits and says Not enough fill blocks. Claims are asked like when mining; the comparator only gives 15 once the pit is filled.
scc.guide.quarry.safe1: Bedrock and everything unbreakable, chests and other blocks with items inside, blocks of the SCC network.
scc.guide.quarry.safe2: It mines as the player who placed it: claim mods (FTB Chunks and others) decide the same way they would for you. Protected blocks are skipped.
scc.guide.quarry.safe3: While it runs it keeps its own chunk loaded (server setting quarryLoadsOwnChunk, on by default) - walk away and the pit still gets finished. A few seconds after it pauses, finishes or is stopped by redstone it lets the chunk go. The chunk it is mining it keeps loaded too (at most two chunks, server setting quarryLoadsWorkChunk), so even a 1000×1000 field gets done. With that setting off it skips unloaded chunks and comes back to them once they are loaded.
scc.guide.quarry.silk: Silk Touch - ores come out as blocks (+50% FE).
scc.guide.quarry.survey: Quarry Survey Tool - picks the area right in the world. Hold it to see glowing boxes.
scc.guide.quarry.survey1: Shift + right-click the quarry to link it: a box in the tier's color shows how far it reaches.
scc.guide.quarry.survey2: Shift + right-click a block for corner A, then one for corner B. The higher one is the top layer; the area goes as deep as the tier allows (down to bedrock on the big tiers). The block you look at lights up green when it works and red when it is out of reach.
scc.guide.quarry.survey3: Right-click opens a window with sliders for offset and size; Shift + right-click the air clears the points.
scc.guide.quarry.survey4: Put the tool into the survey slot of the quarry (left of your inventory): the area is applied at once. While the tool sits there each side may be 1.5 times as long as the tier allows (server setting quarrySurveyBonus) - the Singularity reaches 1500×1500.
scc.guide.quarry.survey5: Quarry Markers from older versions are retired; breaking one gives you a Survey Tool.
scc.guide.quarry.tiers2: From Neutron Star on several layers are cut at once. On the Singularity a black hole replaces the star and swallows two columns of three layers per tick. Basic mines like an iron pickaxe, Red Dwarf and Yellow Star like diamond, from Blue Giant on like netherite.
scc.guide.quarry.void: Void - cobblestone, dirt, netherrack, deepslate and friends vanish (item tag scc:quarry_void, +10% FE).
scc.guide.quarry.what: Mines a whole area layer by layer. A small star hovers above the pit and cuts block after block with lasers; the blocks fly up into it. Six tiers like every device, upgraded in the Star Forge or with an upgrade stone.
scc.guide.quarry.what2: Place the core at the edge of the pit you want: its front faces you, the area lies behind it. Right-click it for the window: the area on the left, a top view on the right, card slots, buffer, progress and the ores below.
scc.guide.recipes.block1: Ctrl+Shift+right-click an item in the terminal to block it. A blocked recipe is never used for planning again, which is how you get rid of a loop the calculator keeps choosing over the route you actually wanted.
scc.guide.recipes.cat1: Everything the mod can plan comes out of one catalogue of recipes, and that catalogue is built from JEI - which means it is built on your client, not on the server. It is written to disk and reused, so normally it is built once per pack.
scc.guide.recipes.cat2: It rebuilds itself when something that matters changes: the mod list, a mod version, or a recipe you blocked.
scc.guide.recipes.jei1: While a terminal is open, ingredients in a JEI or EMI recipe that are not in storage are marked red.
scc.guide.recipes.materials1: Many recipes accept several kinds - any planks, any logs, any stone. In the controller (Recipes tab, page Materials) you set which kind the network takes first, for example always Oak.
scc.guide.recipes.materials2: The planner takes the first kind of the list that is in stock or can be made from stock. If none is enough, it chooses as usual - the list never makes an order fail.
scc.guide.recipes.materials3: Besides the list for all ingredients there can be a list per tag (e.g. #minecraft:planks); a tag list is used first. In the craft tree of the order window, Shift-click a kind in the ingredient choice to put it at the top.
scc.guide.recipes.materials4: A choice for one single ingredient (the four squares in the craft tree) still wins over the list.
scc.guide.recipes.netrules: Recipe rules for the whole network
scc.guide.recipes.netrules1: Recipe and machine choices you make in the order window are saved in the Calculator Controller and apply to every order on this network: other players, Requesters, order lists and AE2 requests. Changing them needs the right to change blocks.
scc.guide.recipes.netrules2: Click a recipe card: always use this recipe. Click the machine on a card: only this machine runs that recipe type.
scc.guide.recipes.netrules3: Shift-click a card: try its recipe type first. Do it again on another card to build an order, e.g. 1 Mekanism, 2 Create.
scc.guide.recipes.netrules4: Right-click a card: never use this recipe type for this item (e.g. never the Furnace for ore blocks). Right-click again to allow it.
scc.guide.recipes.netrules5: The controller tab Recipes lists all rules with who changed them last. Click one to reorder its types, switch "never" on or off, or delete it. A card marked "Network rule" in the order window shows a rule is in effect.
scc.guide.recipes.rescan1: Re-scan recipes in the terminal's menu (the three dots blink when it is due) rebuilds it by hand. You need it after blocking or unblocking a recipe - blocking has no effect until the catalogue has been rebuilt. Block several first and re-scan once; that is the cheaper way round.
scc.guide.recipes.tags1: Pack makers can say which machine runs a recipe category without touching code: the item tag #scc:catalyst/<namespace>/<path> adds machines for the category <namespace>:<path>, #scc:not_catalyst/... removes them. Takes effect on /reload, no rescan.
scc.guide.recipes.why1: Ctrl+middle-click an item in the terminal answers exactly that: what is missing, and how much of it. For a harder case, open the order window - it lists the missing items together with the step that needs them.
scc.guide.singularity.config: All numbers can be changed with /scc - see the Power & Config chapter.
scc.guide.singularity.intro: The top of the ladder. Every Singularity block is faster than a Neutron Star one and has a power of its own:
scc.guide.singularity.p.breaking: Breaking Calculator - Stasis: the tool in it never wears out. On every lower tier it loses durability like in your hand, one point per block (Unbreaking helps).
scc.guide.singularity.p.crafter: Calculation Crafter - Event Horizon: single-step crafts finish in the tick they arrive, independent steps run in the same tick.
scc.guide.singularity.p.never_empty: Processing Calculator, with or without modules - Never Empty: the next batch goes in while the last one is still cooking. A Lock set to Result or Empty switches it off - then it is one batch at a time.
scc.guide.singularity.p.processing: Processing Calculator, with or without modules - Time Dilation: the machine in front runs 2, 4 or 8 times as fast. Pick the step with the clock button in the settings window (right-click goes back). It costs Chronon from the network for every second the machine really runs faster: 1 per second for 2x, 4 for 4x, 16 for 8x (settings: chrononCost2x, chrononCost4x, chrononCost8x; timeDilation caps the speed). Without Chronon the machine simply runs at normal speed. Chronon comes from a black hole in the Stellar Cradle. Machines in the tag scc:no_time_dilation are left alone.
scc.guide.singularity.p.storage: Storage blocks - no limit at all.
scc.guide.singularity.p.transfer: Transfer Calculator - Wormhole: moves the whole inventory every pass (setting: wormholeCap).
scc.guide.sky.bonus.height: The higher an object stands, the more it gives - and the thicker and brighter its beam.
scc.guide.sky.bonus.neutron: The Neutron Star gives double at full moon.
scc.guide.sky.bonus.singularity: The Singularity gives double at new moon.
scc.guide.sky.bonus.yellow: The Yellow Star gives half again as much by day.
scc.guide.sky.chart: The Star Chart: right-click it to see which objects stand high now and next, the moon phase, the next conjunction with a countdown, and a photon forecast for any lens over the next Minecraft day.
scc.guide.sky.chart2: Crafted from an empty map, two amethyst shards and two gold nuggets. All times are real time.
scc.guide.sky.conjunctions1: About once an hour two objects meet in the sky and a soft glow joins them. For 10 minutes every Sky Harvester gets double from both - matter and photons. A notice comes a minute before it starts.
scc.guide.sky.conjunctions2: Five pairs can meet - the ones whose paths lie close together. The Star Chart counts down to the next one. Admins can switch them off with conjunctions in config/scc-server.json.
scc.guide.sky.harvester: A three-block tower: the harvester, two Harvester Masts on top, and a lens floating at the tip. Connect it with a cable and it sends what it harvests straight into the network.
scc.guide.sky.harvester2: It needs open sky above the lens and no rain. It harvests every second, a little from each object its lens reaches. With no network or a full one, the matter piles up in its own slots. The sky objects stand where the Overworld sky is drawn and in space - Ad Astra's planets and orbits count too. Not in the Nether, the End or other dimensions with a sky of their own, such as the Twilight Forest; pack makers can add dimensions with the dimension type tag scc:sky_objects.
scc.guide.sky.harvester3: Right-click it for the sky map: the whole sky seen from below, with the beams that are running.
scc.guide.sky.harvester4: Once the tower stands, it forms into one machine: a turning lattice with a glowing core and a claw at the top that holds the lens. At night the tip lights up while it harvests.
scc.guide.sky.harvester5: No sky at all, as in StoneBlock? A server admin can allow harvesting without sky: /scc skyHarvesterNoSky on. The harvester then also works under a roof and in dimensions without sky objects, but uses twice the power (/scc skyHarvesterNoSkyCost, in percent). Matter only - photon mode still needs real starlight.
scc.guide.sky.lenses1: The lens decides how many objects the harvester reaches: the Basic lens only the Red Dwarf, every tier one more, the Neutron Star lens all five. The Singularity lens reaches the same five but harvests 3.5 times as fast - with black beams.
scc.guide.sky.lenses2: Take the lens out, forge it one tier up, put it back in. The tower stays where it is. Every tier is hungrier: while harvesting, the Basic lens draws 40 FE/t, then 160, 500, 1,500, 4,000 - and the Singularity lens 12,000 FE/t. For three times the power of the Neutron Star lens it harvests 3.5 times as much, so every piece of matter costs less. The power comes from the Energy Storages first, then from the controller, which always keeps a reserve for the network. Without enough power the harvester waits; the network stays on.
scc.guide.sky.lenses3: The Basic lens is the one you craft: glass, amethyst shards and a gold ingot - cheap on purpose, so photon mode can power your first network without any other mod. Every lens above it is forged. The Star Forge itself takes a Nether Star.
scc.guide.sky.o.blue_giant: Blue Giant - large and blue, swings wide
scc.guide.sky.o.neutron_star: Neutron Star - tiny, pulses softly, two slowly turning beams
scc.guide.sky.o.red_dwarf: Red Dwarf - small and red, close to the pole
scc.guide.sky.o.singularity: Singularity - a black hole with a glowing ring and a bent disc of light
scc.guide.sky.objects1: Look north at night. Five objects circle the pole, and none of them ever sets:
scc.guide.sky.objects2: They are visible by day too, just paler. Turn them off with skyObjects in config/scc-client.json if a shader draws its own sky.
scc.guide.sky.objects3: They also wander slowly against each other, like planets - a few degrees a day. Now and then two of them meet: a conjunction.
scc.guide.sky.photons1: Switch the harvester to photon mode with the button on the left of its window. It then harvests no matter; it collects the light of its objects and feeds it into the network as power - first into the controller, then into Energy Storages. It needs no power itself, so it can start an empty network.
scc.guide.sky.photons2: Per lens: 50, 120, 300, 600, 1,000 and 1,600 FE/t, times the height of its objects and the same bonuses as for matter. The Basic lens only sees the Red Dwarf, which always stands high: 50 to 70 FE/t, enough for a small network and a second harvester on matter.
scc.guide.sky.photons3: Harvesters in photon mode within 16 blocks share the sky: the best gets everything, the next half, the third a quarter. Rain gives nothing.
scc.guide.sky.prism.horizon: Event Horizon Prism: 8 Dark Matter and a Chronon. Four raise the lens to Singularity. Chronon comes from a black hole in the Stellar Cradle - and that needs only the Neutron Star lens.
scc.guide.sky.prism.plasma: Plasma Prism: 8 Blue Plasma and a Dragon's Breath. One raises the lens to Blue Giant.
scc.guide.sky.prism.pulsar: Pulsar Prism: 8 Neutronium and an Echo Shard. Two raise the lens to Neutron Star.
scc.guide.sky.prism.solar: Solar Prism: 4 Sun Core, 3 Blaze Powder and a Blaze Rod. One raises the lens to Yellow Star.
scc.guide.sky.prisms1: The Red Dwarf lens is forged from the Basic lens and 2 Red Dwarf Ember. From the Yellow Star lens up, raw matter is no longer enough: the matter the previous lens harvests is bound into a prism at the crafting table, together with something from another corner of the game. The prism then raises the lens in the Star Forge.
scc.guide.sky.prisms2: Pack makers can swap every ingredient: the prism recipes use the item tags scc:lens_prism/<prism>/<part>, for example scc:lens_prism/plasma/catalyst for the Dragon's Breath. Lenses you already have stay as they are.
scc.guide.sky.spyglass: Look at a sky object through a Spyglass and a small sign under the crosshair names it: what it gives, how high it stands, how much a harvester gets from it right now, when it stands highest and whether it is in a conjunction. It shows as long as the sky objects are switched on in the SCC settings.
scc.guide.special.breaking: Breaks blocks out of storage and gives you the real drops. It takes one filtered block at a time, hands it to the game and asks what mining it would produce - so every rule that holds in the world holds here: Fortune multiplies ore, Silk Touch returns the block itself, and a mod with its own loot table gets exactly its own loot.
scc.guide.special.breaking2: Put a tool in it. Every tier adds one level of Fortune on top of that tool - but only if the tool has Fortune at all. A plain pickaxe stays a plain pickaxe. The tool wears out one point per block, like in your hand (Unbreaking helps); only the Singularity keeps it whole. With Keep tool on (the default) it stops at one point left instead of breaking the tool - repair it or swap it, and it goes on. A tool with Mending repairs itself from liquid experience in the network (any fluid tagged c:experience), just like with the wireless terminal.
scc.guide.special.breaking3: Everything mined goes into the inventory above the block. If nothing fits up there, nothing is mined - so nothing is ever lost.
scc.guide.special.breaking4: A filter slot takes a single block or a whole tag. Click a block into the slot, then scroll over it to step through that block's tags - c:ores, minecraft:logs - and back to the block itself. A tag does not name one block, so it is resolved against what is actually in the network: of every stored kind that carries the tag and can be placed as a block, one after another is taken, so c:ores clears out all your ores instead of only the first one. If none of them is in storage, that slot simply contributes nothing.
scc.guide.special.gooey: Only useful with Just Dire Things. The goo blocks of that mod have no inventory - they transform blocks lying next to them in the world, which a network cannot use. This block reproduces the transformation: ingredient out of storage, result straight back in. The goo block in its slot sets the tier, and with it which recipes are possible at all; it is not consumed.
scc.guide.special.transfer: Moves items between the network and the container in front of it. Import, export and both are one block with a switch, so getting it the wrong way round is a click and not a rebuild. The two directions have separate filter lists on purpose: pulling results out of a furnace and putting coal back in are not the same list. A blacklist exists for import only - 'everything except this' makes no sense as an export instruction.
scc.guide.special.transfer2: Every filter entry can also keep a minimum in place: 'leave 8' exports until eight are in the container and imports until eight are left in it. That is how you keep a fuel slot topped up without emptying it, or pull a furnace's output while leaving the stack that is still smelting. It can also order whatever it is supposed to export but does not have, which turns it into an automatic supply line for another mod's machine.
scc.guide.special.transfer_sides: The Sides button swaps the filters for the sides of the machine in front. Per side and per kind (items, fluids, chemicals): input fills the machine from the network using the export list, output takes from it using the import list. On Automatic only the side the calculator touches works, as before. With it one calculator keeps a machine running for good - for example water into an Electrolytic Separator on one side, hydrogen and oxygen out on two others.
scc.guide.special.transform: Also Just Dire Things. Input fluid from the network's tanks, catalyst item from storage, result back into storage as a filled bucket. There is nothing to set up - it only has to be on the network for those transformations to count as possible.
scc.guide.special.wormhole: Jumps to any other Wormhole Gate on the same network. Right-click it: the list shows every gate by name, with its dimension, distance and price. Click one and you arrive standing on top of it, under a small rift. Name a gate in its window (or in an anvil before placing it) - the name is what every other gate lists.
scc.guide.special.wormhole2: Every jump is paid in FE from the network of the gate you leave: 1,000 FE plus 10 FE per block within one dimension, a flat 50,000 FE into another dimension (settings: wormholeBase, wormholePerBlock, wormholeDimension; powerFactor applies). Like the Star Forge it only takes what is above the controller's reserve, so a jump never switches the network off. With power mode off it is free.
scc.guide.special.wormhole3: Gates in other dimensions join the list as soon as the network reaches there - a Wireless Transmitter with a Dimensional Upgrade and a Receiver on the far side. A gate stays listed while its chunk sleeps; the jump loads it. Leashed animals travel along (wormholeLeashed), and after a jump you wait a few seconds (wormholeCooldown).
scc.guide.special.wormhole4: You arrive on top of the target gate. If it is walled in, a safe spot within two blocks is used - solid ground, room to stand, no lava. If there is none, the jump is refused before any power is spent. With security on, jumping needs the build right on the network.
scc.guide.special.wormhole_preview: Look into a running gate and you see the other side: the middle of the tunnel shows the destination like a window - walk past and the view shifts with you. A gate shows the destination you last jumped to (otherwise the first one in its list); a Remote's rift shows its own target. Only blocks are shown (no creatures, no chest contents), and only to players who may use the gate. If the destination is not loaded, you see the last picture, slightly dimmed. Turn it off under F7 (Wormhole preview); it also rests under a shader pack and at very low frame rates. Server owners can switch it off with wormholePreview.
